Content:
A tree is an undirected connected simple graph with no cycles; a graph with no cycles is acyclic.

Content:
A forest is an undirected simple graph with no cycles. Equivalently, a forest is an undirected simple graph whose connected components are trees, hence the name.

Content:
A tree with [MATH: N] vertices always has exactly [MATH: N-1] edges. This provides a useful criterion for identifying trees: a connected graph with [MATH: N] vertices and [MATH: N-1] edges is necessarily a tree.

Content:
For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/84c92a6b0268a8cf320c2c4e60ba1c1e]

Content:
This undirected simple graph is connected and acyclic, so it is a tree. It has [MATH: 4] vertices and [MATH: 3] edges. However, adding any edge introduces a cycle, making it no longer a tree, as illustrated below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2007dfb9ffe710beecf7e4cefdb95f1f]

Content:
Indeed, the graph above is not a tree because it contains a cycle: [MATH: v_1-v_2-v_4-v_1].

A tree with [MATH: N] vertices always has exactly [MATH: N-1] edges. This leads to an alternative definition of a tree, which also serves as a criterion for verifying whether a given graph is a tree: a tree is a connected graph where the number of edges is one less than the number of vertices.

Notice that the given graph is connected but contains the cycle [MATH: v_1-v_2-v_3-v_4-v_5-v_1.]

Recall that a subgraph of a graph [MATH: G] is called a spanning tree of [MATH: G] if it is a tree that includes all the vertices of [MATH: G.]

A spanning tree of a weighted graph with the minimum weight is called a minimum spanning tree (MST). Like any other spanning tree, the MST for a weighted graph with [MATH: N] vertices must have [MATH: N-1] edges.

Our graph has one cycle with [MATH: 4] edges. Hence, to obtain a minimum spanning tree, we need to remove one of the edges from the cycle:

  • First, by removing the edge with a weight of [MATH: 10] we obtain the following tree with a total weight of [MATH: 9+6+7+2+3+8+4 = 39.]

  • Second, by removing the edge with a weight of [MATH: 2] we obtain the following tree with a total weight of [MATH: 9 +6+7+3+8+10+4 = 47.]

  • Third, by removing the edge with a weight of [MATH: 6] we obtain the following tree with a total weight of [MATH: 9+7+2+3+8+10+4 = 43.]

  • Finally, by removing the edge with a weight of [MATH: 3] we obtain the following tree with a total weight of [MATH: 9+6+7+2+8+10+4 = 46.]

Therefore, the minimum spanning tree has a weight of [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}39}.]
